stem.text: Let \( f(x) = - x^{2} \cos{\left(\frac{1}{x} \right)} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \). Find \( \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) \), and justify your answer.

answer_key.label: The limit is -1, because \( -1 - x^{2} \le f(x) \le x^{2} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \) and both bounds approach -1 as x approaches 0.

worked_solution.text: Multiplying by the nonnegative quantity \( x^{2} \) and adding -1 gives \( -1 - x^{2} \le f(x) \le x^{2} - 1 \). The factor \( - x^{2} \) can be negative, so its absolute value is used to keep the inequality true.
Both bounds are continuous, so their limits as x approaches 0 are both -1.

options.label: The limit is -1, because \( -1 - x^{2} \le f(x) \le x^{2} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \), and bounds that are equal at x = 0 force that limit, whatever their limits.
options.derivation: the bounding functions evaluated at the target instead of their limits being taken

options.label: The limit is -1, because \( x^{2} - 1 \le f(x) \le - x^{2} - 1 \) for \( x \ne 0 \) and both bounds approach -1 as x approaches 0.

options.label: The limit is -1, because \( - x^{2} \) approaches 0 and \( \cos{\left(\frac{1}{x} \right)} \) approaches a limit as x approaches 0, so the product theorem applies.
